outline.description: This chapter introduces the Office of Special Counsel (OSC), its statutory authority regarding Fair Civil Service and FOIA enforcement, and the specific factual background of AFL's dispute. Students will learn the obligations of OSC under 5 U.S.C. § 1216 and the specific circumstances triggering AFL's request and subsequent litigation.
subtopics: Overview of the Office of Special Counsel (OSC) and 5 U.S.C. § 1216 authority
OSC enforcement powers under the Civil Service Reform Act for Custodial Practice (PPP) and investigative proceedings
FOIA enforcement provisions under 5 U.S.C. § 552(a)(4)(F)(i) and its relationship to OSC authority
Factual background: AFL's request for DOJ emails and the initial lawsuit
Development of the dispute: DOJ's production of records versus OSC's disclaiming authority
Summary of the District Court's initial rulings on the merits versus procedural dismissal

outline.chapter_title: Procedural Posture and the Standing Threshold
outline.description: This chapter details the procedural history, from the District Court through the circuit court's decision to open supplemental briefing on Article III standing. It explains why the Court of Appeals considered standing a threshold jurisdictional question before addressing the merits, highlighting the unique role of OSC in federal litigation.
subtopics: The District Court's mixed rulings: compliance with statute versus OSC discretion
Remand to OSC and the subsequent final refusal to investigate
Appellate jurisdiction and the order for supplemental briefing on Article III standing
The constitutional basis for standing: Article III 'Case or Controversy' requirement
The difficulty of standing claims against administrative agencies and discretionary decisions
The court's reversal of course: moving from merits determination to jurisdictional dismissal

outline.chapter_title: Article III Standing Analysis: Injury, Causation, and Redressability
outline.description: This chapter provides a deep dive into the Court's analysis of the Article III requirements using the *Lujan* framework. It breaks down AFL's two primary standing theories—informational injury from DOJ's FOIA denial and procedural injury from OSC's statutory refusal—and why each failed to meet the constitutional threshold for Article III jurisdiction.
subtopics: The Article III standing triad: injury in fact, causation, and redressability (*Lujan v. Defenders of Wildlife*)
Theory 1: Informational injury regarding DOJ's FOIA withholding (Injury and Causation)
Analysis of speculative causation: the chain involving MSPB and DOJ choices (*FDA v. Alliance for Hippocratic Medicine*)
Theory 2: Procedural injury regarding OSC's failure to enforce (Procedural Right in Vacuo)
Summers v. Earth Island Institute: procedural rights and concrete interests
Latticeley/Carson precedent on OSC 5 U.S.C. § 1214 notice requirements under § 1216 investigations
Redressability failure: the lack of entitlement to OSC investigative findings under § 1216
The legal principle of agency discretion (*Heckler v. Chaney*) and judicial compulsion limits

outline.description: This chapter outlines the final outcome of the appeal, explaining the specific remedy granted to AFL and why the server-citigability was the final word. It contextualizes this decision for law students regarding future litigation strategies concerning OSC investigations and FOIA enforcement.
subtopics: Vacatur of the District Court judgment and remand with instructions to dismiss for lack of subject-matter jurisdiction
Implications for the OSC's discretionary enforcement power
Limitations on non-government plaintiffs seeking OSC investigations of administrative policies
The distinction between statutory interpretation and constitutional adjudication in administrative suits
Rejection of the specific FOIA injury theory versus procedural injury theory as equally failing to meet standing
